passages.t: The ark and the mercy seat
passages.happening:
“Bezalel went on to construct the ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high. He overlaid it with pure gold, both inside and out” (verses 1-2). He makes rings and poles to carry it (verses 3-5).

“He constructed a mercy seat of pure gold” (verse 6), with two cherubim of hammered gold at its ends. “And the cherubim had wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat. The cherubim faced each other, looking toward the mercy seat” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
With the tent made, the work moves inside, to the things that will stand in God's house. They are made in order from the center outward: first the ark, for the inner room, then the table, the lampstand and the altar of incense, for the Holy Place.

This chapter follows 25:10-40 closely, and the notes on chapter 25 describe each piece. One thing is different. The plans gave the purpose of each thing. Here those lines are left out. The chapter does not repeat God's promise to meet Moses above the mercy seat (25:22). The reader already knows what these things are for. What matters now is that they were made, exactly, in pure gold.

Here Bezalel is named as the maker (verse 1).

The ark is a chest about 45 inches long and 27 inches wide and high, small enough for four men to carry on poles. Its form belonged to its world. Egypt had sacred chests with carrying poles, and its art shows winged figures spreading their wings over a shrine. Its meaning did not belong to that world. The ark held no image of a god. It held written words: the stone tablets of the covenant, the same words the people broke with the calf and God wrote again.

Kings of that age sat on thrones with winged guardians at each side and rested their feet on a footstool. The cherubim over the ark form the throne of a King who cannot be seen. Where other peoples would have set a statue, there is empty space.
passages.later:
The Bible speaks of the LORD “who sits enthroned between the cherubim” (1 Samuel 4:4), and a psalm calls the ark his footstool: “let us worship at His footstool” (Psalm 132:7).

When Solomon brought the ark into the temple, “There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb” (1 Kings 8:9).

Paul uses the Greek word for the mercy seat of Jesus: “God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood” (Romans 3:25). Hebrews names “the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the mercy seat” (Hebrews 9:5).
passages.hard:
What happened to the ark of the covenant?

The Bible does not say. The ark is placed in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:6), and it is mentioned again in the days of King Josiah, late in the seventh century BC (2 Chronicles 35:3). When the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, the list of temple objects they carried off does not name it (2 Kings 25:13-17). Most historians think it was destroyed or taken then, or perhaps earlier.

Later traditions filled the gap. The book of 2 Maccabees tells a legend that Jeremiah hid the ark in a cave. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church holds that it rests in a chapel at Aksum, though no outsider has been allowed to examine what is there. No evidence supports the modern claims that it has been found.

Jeremiah himself looked ahead to a day when the ark would not be missed: “It will never come to mind, and no one will remember it or miss it, nor will another one be made” (Jeremiah 3:16). The New Testament's interest lies elsewhere. In John's vision, “the temple of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of His covenant appeared in His temple” (Revelation 11:19).
passages.asks: At the center of Israel's worship was a chest of God's words under a seat of mercy. Ask what stands at the center of your own worship. And ask whether you could lose every holy object you treasure and still have God himself.

passages.happening:
“He also made the table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. He overlaid it with pure gold and made a gold molding around it” (verses 10-11). It has a rim, rings and poles (verses 12-15).

“He also made the utensils for the table out of pure gold: its plates and dishes, as well as its bowls and pitchers for pouring drink offerings” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The table stood in the Holy Place, in front of the veil. On it would lie the Bread of the Presence: twelve loaves, renewed every Sabbath, set out before God on behalf of the whole people and then eaten by the priests.

Other nations set meals before the statues of their gods. Israel's God had no statue and needed no feeding. The bread on this table was set out ‘on behalf of the Israelites’, as a sign of the covenant.

The note on 25:23-30 says more.
passages.later:
Leviticus gives the rule for the bread: “Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant” (Leviticus 24:8).

Jesus said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). He does not point to this table, so the link is one of theme.
passages.asks: The table kept bread before God week after week. Ask what you bring before God regularly, not only in a crisis. And ask whether you thank him for ordinary bread.

passages.happening:
“Then he made the lampstand out of pure hammered gold, all of one piece: its base and shaft, its cups, and its buds and petals. Six branches extended from the sides, three on one side and three on the other” (verses 17-18). Its cups are “shaped like almond blossoms” (verse 19).

“He also made its seven lamps, its wick trimmers, and trays of pure gold. He made the lampstand and all its utensils from a talent of pure gold” (verses 23-24).
passages.hearers:
The lampstand, menorah in Hebrew, is shaped like an almond tree in flower, hammered from one piece of gold. A talent of gold is usually reckoned at about 75 pounds, or 34 kilograms.

The almond is the first tree to blossom in the land of Israel, in late winter. Many interpreters see in the lampstand a picture of the tree of life, its light burning before God through the night.

The Hebrew word for ‘shaped like almond blossoms’ is related to a verb that means to watch or stay awake. Jeremiah plays on the link when he sees an almond branch and God says he is watching over his word.

The seven-branched lampstand became one of the most lasting signs of the Jewish people. The lampstand of the later temple can still be seen carved on the Arch of Titus in Rome, carried off among the spoils after the temple fell in AD 70.
passages.later:
God asked Jeremiah what he saw. “I see a branch of an almond tree,” he said, and God answered, “I am watching over My word to accomplish it” (Jeremiah 1:11-12).

The prophet Zechariah saw “a solid gold lampstand” with seven lamps on it (Zechariah 4:2). John saw “seven golden lampstands” and the risen Christ among them (Revelation 1:12-13).
passages.asks: The lamp was shaped like the first tree to wake after winter. Ask where you need to believe that God is awake and watching over his word to you. And ask what small light you have been given to keep burning.

passages.t: The altar of incense, the oil and the incense
passages.happening:
“He made the altar of incense out of acacia wood. It was square, a cubit long, a cubit wide, and two cubits high. Its horns were of one piece” (verse 25). He overlays it with pure gold and makes rings and poles for it (verses 26-28).

“He also made the sacred anointing oil and the pure, fragrant incense, the work of a perfumer” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
In the plans, the altar of incense came late, in chapter 30, after everything else. Here it takes its place with the other golden furniture of the Holy Place, where it belongs.

It stood just in front of the veil. Every morning and evening the priest burned incense on it as he tended the lamps (30:7-8).

One verse covers the oil and the incense, which took up much of chapter 30. The note there describes the spices and explains why the recipes were kept for God alone.

Now all the furniture for inside the tent is made. Chapter 38 moves out into the courtyard.
passages.later:
A psalm makes incense a picture of prayer: “May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering” (Psalm 141:2).

In Revelation an angel is given incense to offer “along with the prayers of all the saints, on the golden altar before the throne” (Revelation 8:3).
passages.asks: Incense rose before God every morning and evening. Ask what part prayer has at the start and end of your days. And ask whether you believe your prayers rise before God, as Revelation pictures them.
